utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon. The Chamber is again sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis, in the absence of Judge Mindua, as indicated earlier. The witness should be brought in, please. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Judge Nyambe. Just on -- it was P200 -- 2200, the one where I had a different translation, I am told the one in e-court was the proper translation so I had the wrong one, so we're fine the way we are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry, it's P2200.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now we have it correct. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Welcome back to the courtroom. I have to remind you that the affirmation to tell the truth you made at the beginning of your testimony still applies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey has additional questions for you. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you recall helping one of our investigators, several years ago now, in giving them help in diagramming where the different offices were at Crna Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And have you recently had a chance to look at that diagram that the investigator made?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's take a quick look at that. It's 65 ter 07344. And, Mr. President, for some reason this did not get a 65 ter number. We used it at the site visit, so it's -- I don't think there's any problem, and if we could just show this to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Leave is granted to add it to the 65 ter exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if we could go to the next page, that's the -- just the investigative page that talks about when this happened back in 2006. And perhaps we can blow up especially that B/C/S side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I think you said something, that this was your best recollection, but you couldn't be positive. As you look at it now, how do you -- how confident you are that that's where the basic offices were?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that this is -- and I must say that I'm even less certain now than I was before, but I think this is how it was. The things there changed. We didn't have enough space for all of us, and there was re-shuffling. Some people went to a hotel in Pijesak, some of the people were in this building. But I think this is roughly it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And the Chamber has been there and seen those two long wooden buildings that were next to each other, and let me just direct your attention to the left -- the left one. And we see that Salapura -- that's your office at the top of the page?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And we also see, if we look at the English, underneath your office it says "Intel Office." Who was in there?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Analysts. And there was a clerk there, warrant officer, as well as all the analysts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: For example --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I spent most of my time there. I was not very often in my office, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you've mentioned Analyst Radoslav Jankovic. Was he there?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Mamlic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Jankovic, Mamlic, Karanovic, Isakovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And when General Mladic was in Crna Rijeka, what office, if any, did he work out of?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was using the offices -- rather, this room number 6, the meeting room next to Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I would offer this exhibit into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit P2201, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Colonel, when did you first become aware that there was a VRS attack on the Srebrenica enclave? I'm talking the one that started July 6th.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was on the 12th that I learned about it, when I was in Modrica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And as I recall, you said you first left Banja Luka on -- is it July 11th?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, on the 12th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where did you go on the 12th?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Banja Luka, Modrica, Bijeljina, [indiscernible].

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you tell us where Modrica is? What corps was that in?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1st Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I ask you to repeat. You mentioned four locations, Banja Luka, Modrica, Bijeljina, and then another one, but we couldn't hear the interpreters with this word. What was the fourth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Beograd, Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Could we have 65 ter 5692. This is a document that I was given last night, so it may not be on the list. Oh, it is on the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I know this was a while back, Colonel, but we see the document is dated 1 July, from the Main Staff Intelligence and Security Sector, Intelligence Administration, and it's talking about these two men getting moved over to Bijeljina. And if we can go to the next page in the English, and show the bottom of the page in the B/C/S. Now, we see this is a teletype, so, of course, there's no signature on this version of it. Does this help refresh your recollection where you were on 1 July?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. This -- something like this, the content of this document does not remind me of anything. Why would I have written something like that? And, anyway, I didn't sign it. I cannot see any signature here. I don't know what this is. This is about some people I don't know. I only heard of, I think, Bratic, Radivoje. I have no idea what this is all about, secretariats in Bijeljina and Trebinje, no. At the time, I was in Banja Luka, definitely. It is possible that it was sent -- I see "SM/SM." That's Slobodan Mamlic. He might have drafted this, based on the initials. You can see both of them as the drafter and the one who sent it, and then put my signature. But as you can see, I did not sign this document. It should have been "for," at least. Water Supply Directorate, no, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, sir, we see this is a received document. So, as you know, a teletype never has a signature. It's not like a fax. Perhaps you called up Mamlic and authorised him --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Right. So perhaps you called up Mamlic and had him -- and you authorised him to send this out, or perhaps you allowed people to send material out in your name, without knowing about it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly did not call Mamlic about this. I can't remember any of these things, what were my connections with the people who were in charge of water supply. Palma, what is this: "Please send Engineer Saric, Dragan, Bratic, Radivoje, to VP Bijeljina. They would be engaged that for a period of 10 days at most." I don't even know what this is all about. I can't even figure out from the contents what it's all about. I don't remember any of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So you --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Allegedly, it was sent to the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would offer this document in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I ask the witness one question. Sir, you see on the original, on the left side of the screen, a stamp. In the second line on the stamp, you see there are two words. One is crossed out and one is underlined. Could you please tell me what these words mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "RCV, Sent/Received." Well, this stamp was put by the encoding station, the people who were sending the telegrams. These are their markings. As we can see, "Sent" is crossed out, which means that the telegram was received on the 1st of July at 1755 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: So this is the copy which was received by the addressee; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a copy that was handed over on the 1st of July at 1755 hours to the Encoding Service, and it was sent via teletype. There is a "TLP" underlined here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. And could this kind of document bear a signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the original would have had a signature, but this document, this copy, I don't know where it was sent. Could you please put it back on the screen or put it back up so that I can see who the addressee is? Yes, it was sent to the Ministry of Defence, Pale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. This document will be received into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But why, I really can't tell.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P2202, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So why did you leave Banja Luka to go to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to Banja Luka first for treatment. I was ill. But I received an invitation to go to Belgrade for a meeting with a certain person from whom I was expecting to receive certain information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was this a confidential source, this person that you met with?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So who actually alerted you to this? Who called you at Banja Luka? I don't need the name, if it's the confidential informant. Did he just call you up, or did you hear it from one of your people, or someone else?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I received the call or invitation via the Intelligence Centre in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: From what intelligence centre; an army, a corps? Who?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, it was our Main Staff's Intelligence Centre. It had its seat there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who called you?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you now whether it was the chief of centre or somebody else. I can't remember who was it who called me. Actually, I think somebody came to my house with a car to tell me that I'm expected in Belgrade on the 12th. The 12th, in the afternoon or evening hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, did you receive a call from the Intelligence Centre or did someone come by and get you? These are important questions.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information reached me via the Intelligence Centre. I can't tell you now. They didn't call me. Somebody came to my home and informed me about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right, Colonel. Now, you have said that you went to Belgrade and received the actual time and date of the attack planned by the Croatian forces in the Krajina, and we'll get to that, but this is some of the most important information that could be possibly received by an intelligence officer. I'm sure you will agree. So, please, who came by and told you about this, this important information?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hope you don't ask me -- you're not asking me to give you the name, because I don't see how that is related with this case. He's not here today, anyhow, and I cannot give you the name of that person.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm not asking the name of the confidential informant. You said someone came by, in Banja Luka, in a car?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they didn't -- he didn't come to Banja Luka. He came to Belgrade, and I was supposed to meet with this person in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go back to Banja Luka. Who did you first hear from that you were to go to Banja Luka -- that you were to go to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was already in Banja Luka, and people from the centre informed me that I'm supposed to go to Belgrade. The organisation was like this: A person, who had come to Belgrade, called a number, a number that was the number of the Intelligence Centre in Banja Luka, and also there was a number in Han Pijesak, and they were informed at the centre that at a certain hour I was supposed to come to Belgrade. And then somebody from the centre came to my home. They knew that I was there, and they told me, Colonel, you're expected in Belgrade at a certain hour. We've just heard news about that. This was not the first time that I had to do this. There were many occasions like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Try again. Who came to your home in a car to tell you this?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the operatives from the centre, but I really can't remember which one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, roughly, what time of day did you set off from Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the morning, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: With who?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I set off with my driver and with two other officers, reserve officers, IT people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What's your driver's name?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Radan Djukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who were these IT people? Why were they with you?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were supposed to install new programmes at the administration, and they worked at our offices in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where were they to install programmes?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the Main Staff Intelligence Administration in Han Pijesak, in that conference room that you saw on that plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay, and you first go to Modrica. And then from Modrica, where do you go?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: To Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you stop in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And about what time did you get to Bijeljina, just roughly?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was around noon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What part of Bijeljina? Did you go to the East Bosnia Corps Command?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I didn't go to the East Bosnia Corps Command. There was a group from that centre, a group of operatives. There was a kind of group, a sub-unit numbering three persons, who worked there in Modrica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We're talking about Bijeljina now.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry, we had an interpretation error there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so what did you do in Bijeljina, in this Intelligence Centre?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't do anything. I was supposed to leave the IT people there. Then they were supposed to put them in a car in Bijeljina and transport them to Han Pijesak, whereas I continued on to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you and your driver went to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And about what time did you get to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's hard to say. Well, it was after 1600 hours, in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And were you able to meet with the confidential source and receive the information from him or her?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what was the basic information that you received from this source?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croatian Army was to carry out an attack on the Republic of the Serbian Krajina. I think that the date for that was the 1st or the 2nd of August, 1995, using forces from the Zagreb, Split, Rijeka Garrisons and a part of the forces from the Osijek Garrison. The attack was to be against all of the forces of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina from along the area of Lika, Banja and Kordun. What was the most interesting thing was that after the execution of that assignment, they were going to move to attack the forces in the west of Republika Srpska, in co-ordination with forces of the Bosnian Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was anybody else present with you when you received this information from this source?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The driver definitely was not there. He was somewhere else. He was sitting in the car, waiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So then what did you do?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody else is present in these kinds of situations, as a rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So then what did you do?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had another meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Belgrade also.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: With who?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: With a diplomat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: From where?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Belgrade, serving in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you pass on any of the information you had just learned to this diplomat?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What's the name of the diplomat?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We discussed completely different topics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You were asked for the name of the diplomat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm trying to remember. It was the Japanese military attache, but I cannot remember right now, well, if that means anything to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I wish for peace in this house, and I would like these proceedings according to God's will and not according to mine. I wish to greet Mr. Salapura. I wish him a pleasant stay among us. I would like to ask Mr. McCloskey, when he asks about the name of confidential sources or diplomatic representatives, that he would move into private session, not because of us or Mr. Salapura, but because of them, because we're always obliged to maintain the confidentiality of these people. So perhaps we could move into a private session in such cases. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this assistance. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'll take that proposal under advisement, General, though I don't think we're getting a name anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What did you do after your meeting with the military representative from the Japanese Embassy?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I returned to Bijeljina in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Where did you go in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the premises of the centre, where I left these two IT guys earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, roughly, what time did you get there?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I'm really unable to tell you. I mean, I could give you a rough, I don't know, Well, I think. I don't know whether this was at 10.00. Perhaps 2100 hours, 2200 hours. I don't know. I cannot really give you a definite time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so what did you do at this Intelligence Centre in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to sleep, and I was informed that the two IT people, they were not able to take them where they were supposed to go because the vehicle was -- it broke down, so they couldn't take them to Han Pijesak. And so they called me that evening also. Mamlic answered the phone up there. I wanted to speak to Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did they call you or did you call them?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who, did who call me? I'm sorry, I didn't understand. I didn't understand who you were referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You say, "they called me that evening also." My question is: Did Mamlic call you or did you call Mamlic call you?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I called, I called Mamlic, and I said that the IT people had stayed in Bijeljina because they were not able to take them to Han Pijesak. They didn't have a vehicle available. Perhaps that's where the misunderstanding lies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Know then what did you say to Mamlic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asked for Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Why? Why did you want to speak to Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was supposed to convey this information to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you going to convey it over the telephone or however you were speaking to this person? You said you called.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had a secure line from Bijeljina, an encrypted line, so I was able to use it for that. I could transfer messages to Han Pijesak using an encrypted line.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You mean oral communications or encrypted teletype?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, oral communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what did Mamlic tell you when you tried to get -- when you wanted him to bring you Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me that Tolimir was not at the command post, that he was in Rogatica, or, rather, in Zepa, and that he was calling in from time to time from Rogatica, or sent some information or a request from Rogatica occasionally, but that they were not able to get in touch with him. He was able to call from Rogatica, once he came to Rogatica, or to send a message or some information from there if something was needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So by the -- roughly, after 10.00 p.m. on the night of the 12th, you get information that Tolimir is already on his way to the Rogatica/Zepa area?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't get the information that he was on the way there. I received information that he was in Zepa, somewhere in that area. I didn't get information to the effect that he was on his way or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did Mamlic tell you he'd been in Bijeljina that day?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who? No, no, he was calling from time to time. He wasn't calling in every day. That's what he told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So did you make an arrangement for General Tolimir to be able to receive your call through Mamlic, since he was calling in at times?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, that was the conversation, and so now I asked him where General Mladic was, could I speak to him. He said he didn't know, he didn't have any contact with him. Of course, he didn't have any contact with him. So now since these people did not take these IT people to Han Pijesak, I decided to go to Han Pijesak the following day to take these two people up there in my own car, and to find the commander and to convey the information to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you convey this simple information you'd received to your subordinate over this secure line, Mamlic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you were the only one that had this information in your head now. Did you write it down?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did have some indications before as well. I didn't write it down anywhere at the time. I just kept it in my head.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: After Mamlic didn't know where Mladic was, did you have him refer you to the ops. room, the ops. people, General Miletic, General Gvero, someone else there? We've seen this happen repeatedly on the intercepts.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you check --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I understand. Did you --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- because -- because I had had decided to take these two people up there, and I was supposed to take them, anyway, the ones who were supposed to have been taken to Han Pijesak that day. Anyway, they didn't have a vehicle, they couldn't transport them that day, so then I decided to take them in my own vehicle and to personally inform the commander, or possibly Tolimir, about this information that was important. And I am bound by the rules to orally state information that was important in decision-making or could affect or bring about a change in decision-making, and I was supposed to orally convey that to the superior, perhaps in case some clarifications were necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You're saying it was more important to take the IT guys to Han Pijesak than try to get Miletic or Gvero on the telephone? Why didn't you try to get Miletic or Gvero on the phone?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why would I try to get in touch with them? In view of the importance of the information, it was my duty to inform the interested person orally and also, along with that, transport these two IT guys --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So why didn't you just get in your car and drive to Han Pijesak? Why did you spend the night there?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, why would I go at night? You could see that I was travelling. I had covered a lot of road. The roads were very difficult at the time, they were full of potholes, worn down. I was quite tired, and also I would like to remind you that my health was not very good at the time. I was not feeling well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So what did you do in the morning? Now we're in the morning of the 13th.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I set off for Han Pijesak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you make any determination on the security situation from the roadway from Bijeljina to Han Pijesak?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you make any effort to find out what was going on with the fall of Srebrenica, its aftermath, the movement of your troops, the movement of the enemy troops, any of the critical intel information that the Main Staff would have been interested in there at the centre, this Intelligence Centre?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Why would I? I mean, that was something the Main Staff should have known about. Somebody up there was probably dealing with that. How was I supposed to get information about that, anyway? Perhaps just ask the villagers along the way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You said you were at an intel centre in Bijeljina. It was an army intel centre, I take it. They would have had intel?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we go to 65 ter 141.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, I believe you've seen this in the other trial, though I'm not -- there is two similar documents. This, as we see, is from the Drina Corps Command Intelligence Department, strictly confidential number 17/896, dated 12 July. It's to the Main Staff of the VRS Sector for Intelligence and Security, to the sector for Intelligence and Security, your Intelligence Administration, and then there's quite a few other --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- addresses we see there, including the MUP, and it's regarding the statement of a prisoner of war, Izudin Bektic. And if we can go to the end of it, I won't spend a lot of time on the intel that Bektic is giving about the 28th Division escaping from Srebrenica. But we see this is from your boss, Major General Zdravko Tolimir, and we see a couple of stamps down there. One is a stamp from the 2nd Romanija Motorised Brigade, which we can see was one of the addressees, dated 13 July.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The other stamp is hard to make out, but it's dated 12 July at 2210 hours. And there's some other times, 2215 on the 12th of July, 2217, so it's an evening that this document is either sent or received from the Drina Corps, under the name of General Tolimir. So what does this suggest to you about the location of General Tolimir on the 12th of July, in the evening?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Well, here, at the Command of the 2nd Romanija Motorised Brigade. I don't know. Can I see the heading of the document again, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The beginning of the document, I would kindly ask if I could see it. Yes, this is from the Command of the 2nd Romanija Brigade, probably sent to the Drina Corps Command. And then from the Drina Corps Command, it was sent to the Intelligence Administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, we can see the top heading, as in all these documents, is the place where the documents originated, isn't that correct, this one being the Drina Corps Command? And from the Drina Corps Command, it was sent to the Main Staff and the other places?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So given that this originated from the Drina Corps Command, does this suggest to you anything about General Tolimir's location on the evening of 12 July?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it doesn't suggest that it's the command. If it states at the bottom that it's the 2nd Romanija Brigade, then it's probably in that brigade, if the document was sent from there. Perhaps he was in Vlasenica. Yes, yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you find any indication, General, that this document was sent from the person it was addressed to, one of the people, the Romanija Brigade? This is just a receipt stamp, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, the IKM of the Drina Corps, the IKM Bratunac. I would just like to read it in detail first, please. This was sent to a number of brigades, one, two, three, four, five, six, to the MUP, to Milici, and to Zvornik for their information, and it was sent from the Drina Corps Command, from the Intelligence Administration there. Perhaps General Tolimir was in Vlasenica at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would offer this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit P2203, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can we now go to D64. And perhaps it would help the colonel if he had a document to look at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher, yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Colonel, we see this is -- begins very similar, from the Command of the Drina Corps, Intelligence Department, and this is strictly confidential number 17/897. And we'll recall that the previous document was 17/896. This is also dated 12 July. And if we go to the next page in the English --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- and the B/C/S --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- we again see that this is in the name of Major-General Zdravko Tolimir. And, again, I don't want to go over the detail of this document, but it provides quite a bit of specific intelligence information regarding Muslim groups, Naser Oric's deputies. And the fifth paragraph down on the first page, if we could go back to the first page --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- it says: "All electronic surveillance units of the SRK IBK," which is the East Bosnia Corps in Bijeljina, "and the Drina Corps shall fucus of surveillance and monitoring radio communications between these Muslim groups which operate on frequency 164800."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, where can we find it in the English version?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Fifth paragraph down, if I've got the -- yes, as I mentioned. I'm sorry, I didn't notice it wasn't up there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And as we see, this was sent to the East Bosnia Corps. And it also says: "The OPB organs of the brigade commands will propose to the commanders of the units positioned along the line of withdrawal of elements of the routed 28th Muslim Division from Srebrenica to undertake all measures to prevent the withdrawal of enemy soldiers ..." Let's go on to the next page. It also makes reference to how the Muslims wish to portray Srebrenica, and it says, well, it's very important to arrest as many members of the shattered Muslim units as possible or liquidate them if they resist. It's equally important to note down the names of all fit men for military service who are being evacuated from the UNPROFOR base in Potocari. And the receipt stamps we see, again from the 2nd Romanija Motorised Brigade, 13 July, but the bottom stamp is 12 July at 2150 hours, and then there's another one processed 2200 hours and sent 2210 hours. So, again, this is the evening of 12 July. Do you know how General Tolimir received this detailed intelligence information? He's got radio frequencies, he knows what's going on in Potocari, he's got information about the Muslim groups. Were you part of the chain of information that he was receiving that day, as you should have been?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it would have been inappropriate for me to be aware of it because it would have been impossible. I was away on a trip. I told you that yesterday. And, second, when I went to Banja Luka, in agreement with my superior, Mr. Tolimir, I went there to deal with one specific problem alone. I was supposed to stay there for a month, and I was also supposed to co-ordinate the work of intelligence organs between the 1st and the 2nd Corps and the centre, as required, whereas General Tolimir took upon himself the work in the eastern parts. So I didn't deal with anything of the kind over there. I did not know that the attack on Srebrenica had been planned or carried out until the 12th, in Modrica. In fact, it was reported by the media before I learned of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, you've said that several times, and I understand.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Therefore -- well, that's why I'm saying it's impossible, because that's the question you asked and I'm trying to explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give an answer to that. I mean, I can speculate, I can guess, but that's your assumption. I'm telling you it's the way it was, and I can tell you about the procedure for obtaining such information. We had an electronic reconnaissance unit in the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's a simple question. Were you part of a chain of information? The answer was, No, and you've explained why. I think we understand. Do you need to explain anything else?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, really not, absolutely not. And you also asked me how General Tolimir was able to get this information and whether I was part of that chain. I am just telling you that the Intelligence Administration also had an electronic reconnaissance unit which was a unit that kept the communications of the enemy under surveillance, and they listen and eavesdrop on radio and radio-relay connections, and the Drina Corps had such a unit like the Eastern Bosnia Corps. They were not all equipped equally well. Some had obsolete equipment. But all corps had their radio reconnaissance units, and they could easily obtain such information from listening to communications on the air. You call it intercepts, and we call it radio reconnaissance. That's our term.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And in the following next few days, the 13th, 14th, 15th, 16th, did you actually receive information from your radio reconnaissance people about the 28th Division that you were able to pass on; you, yourself?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the Main Staff didn't have a unit of its own. Only the corps had electronic reconnaissance units, and only the corps monitored these communications, and they were able to obtain and process such information. The Main Staff -- that is to say, the administration did not have an electronic reconnaissance unit within its composition.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, I was asking you: Did you get information from your subordinate corps, the Drina Corps? Did you, at the Main Staff, get such electronic information from the Drina Corps about the movements of the 28th Division or any intel that you dealt with; you, Colonel Salapura?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, getting --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Getting back to this document, again it's from the Command of the Drina Corps, in the evening, from General Tolimir. Does that suggest to you, especially when you combine the other document with the same origin, that he spent at least some time at Vlasenica on the evening of 12th July?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know to whom this document was sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, let's go to the first page. It's just like the other one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's from the command. It doesn't have as many addressees. We can see that. It's to the Intelligence and Security Departments.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: 12th July. Is this the document numbered 17/897, dated 12 July?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's the one I'm asking about, very similar to the last one.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If that's the document, yes, it was sent from the Command of the Drina Corps, their Intelligence Section.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And it was sent to the Sarajevo Romanija Corps and the Eastern Bosnia Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to 65 ter 7348 [Realtime transcript read in error "3760"]. This also did not have a 65 ter number, so I would request leave of the Court to, based on some answers to my questions, show this to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Leave is granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, we can see this is from the Main Staff, the Intelligence Administration, dated 15 July, very urgent, to the Radio Reconnaissance Platoon of the Drina Corps, to Colonel Mirko Petrovic, personally. Is this your signature at the bottom of this?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is, to the Radio Reconnaissance Platoon. Yes, it is, yes, it's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you were involved?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's probably Mamlic who wrote this, typed it up and gave me to sign, and then I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you were involved with the Drina Corps radio reconnaissance information? Does this help refresh your recollection or are you putting this completely on Mamlic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Mamlic was a desk officer in charge of radio reconnaissance and he was in charge of this job, but this was just an instruction given to other units to jam communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I should point out there's a typo in this English translation. It says the 26th Division, and that should be the 28th Division, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So according to this document, you've issued an instruction to the Drina Corps radio recon people to jam the communications of the scattered group of the 28th Division. We all know that's Naser Oric's group, though he wasn't there, and the forces of the 2nd Corps of the Muslim army, which we know are on the other side of the line --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- and have a task to carry out a co-ordinated operation in the general sector of Zvornik and Sekovici. It's like their own typo, not ours, on the spelling of "Sekovici." Do you agree with that? There's no such place as Sehovici, is there?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Co-ordinated action of forces in the broader area of Zvornik and Sehovici."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So according to this document, you will have been following --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean Sehovici is not there? Sehovici is there, along a different road also leading to Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's not how you spell Sekovici, is it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here, you have an "h" instead of "k."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: My question was: That's just a typo, isn't it? Isn't that meant to be "Sekovici"?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you, having written this document with this information in it, would have been follow the activities of the 15th of July that were going on in the area of Zvornik? The Muslim column, as it was moving from Srebrenica through the zone of Zvornik, passed the area of Sekovici; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I signed this document. This is to turn on the jamming devices. Somebody must have sent a request to Mamlic, and then Mamlic drafted it and gave me it to sign, and later on I found myself at the command post. But the information we received, we did not receive directly from electronic reconnaissance, but we received intelligence reports already processed by the Drina Corps. That's to say we did not receive primary documents, but secondary documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you're back at the -- on the 15th, you're at the Crna Rijeka Command Post, and you're engaged in your intelligence work, and you're following what's going on in Zvornik with the Muslim column; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 15th of July, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Could we go briefly back --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not taking part in the intelligence work. I got involved from time to time, of course I was interested in what was going on, and we were monitoring mainly preparations of the Tuzla Corps for a counter-attack. That was the focus of our attention. But, of course, in the process of monitoring them, you also monitor the other communications. That was on the 15th, and, of course, alongside you monitor the other communications as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you know at the time that on the 15th of July, about 800 prisoners had been summarily executed in the Zvornik area around Orahovac, about 800 had been summarily executed in the Zvornik area around the village of Petkovci, and they were beginning to be executed near the village of Kozluk, at the same time that the Muslim 28th Division is -- you're jamming their communications?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, definitely, and still don't understand to date that such an idea could have been conceived in anyone's head. But I did not know a word about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you know your colleague, Colonel Beara, was working with Zvornik Brigade Security Officer Drago Nikolic in organising and facilitating those summary executions?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, definitely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you know that your colleague in the Drina Corps, Major Pavle Golic, was communicating with Colonel Beara and Drago Nikolic regarding the organisation and the facilitation of those murders?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And were you aware that Colonel Beara was asked to call and report to the Main Staff several times during the days of the 14th, the 15th, the 16th, where you were, Crna Rijeka? Did that make its way to the Intelligence Department or have you just not heard any of that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry. To report about what?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What they were doing, I guess. They were asked to report, report what they were doing in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. That never reached me. I don't know whether that information ever got to other operative organs, but it did not reach me. And my administration and Mamlic certainly did not learn about it, because a thing of this kind he would have reported to me immediately. Whether it had reached General Miletic or someone else, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did your subordinate intelligence analyst, Radoslav Jankovic, who was in Bratunac from the 11th, 12th, 13th, through at least the 18th and 19th, did he send you reports on what he was doing in the Bratunac/Potocari area on those days?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he was at the SFOR base. That's what I was told. He was re-subordinated to the Command of the Drina Corps to serve as a liaison officer at the SFOR base in Potocari, and that's the job he was doing. He was not duty-bound to submit that information to us, but to the Drina Corps Command, but sometimes he would pass on information to the Intelligence Administration of the Main Staff as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, you've seen those documents in the previous trial, when he reported to the Main Staff, Jankovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We'll go over a few of those.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there's one or two.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And could I tender 65 ter 7348?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This would be Exhibit P2204, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. In the chronology, you're in Bijeljina. What do you do in the morning?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When in the morning?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, you get up. Where do you go from Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the toilet. Then I go wash my face and get ready. And then from Bijeljina, I went in the morning -- do you mean the 13th? To Han Pijesak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the 13th. So where did you go on the morning of the 13th?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: To Han Pijesak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you check the security situation on the roadway - that's where we left off - before driving down there?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I never checked that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where can you go?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there was a problem, somebody would have stopped me. They would just stop the car and say, You can't go on, there's something going on further up the road. And I've been through critical situations many times during the war, and nobody -- nobody ever warned me that there was a problem somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so when did you first drive to from Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I went to Han Pijesak, and my first stop was at Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you tell us -- the Judges are familiar with this, but from Bijeljina, up in the north, did you go along the river through Zvornik and then down to Konjevic Polje? Is that the way you went? --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not north, just down the Drina River. Yes, yes, yes, to the right, that's the road I took.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, could you please check the transcript. On page 30, line 21, it is recorded that you have said: "And so when did you first drive to Bijeljina?" Was that really your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It should have been "from Bijeljina." I could have misspoken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you get to Konjevic Polje, and where, precisely, do you go?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, now I have some interference. From Konjevic Polje, when I got there, on the left side there was some sort of stadium. There were quite a few prisoners there. And I headed to the Battalion of the Military Police. That's up towards Kasaba. I wanted to get information about the whereabouts of General Mladic. So I came to the MP Battalion. I believe the battalion commander, Malinic, was there. And then they told me that they didn't know exactly, but he was somewhere in the area of Bratunac, so I headed back and towards Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So was this the 65th Protection Regiment Military Police Battalion?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that was a battalion of the 65th Protection Regiment of the military police. It was a battalion within the 65th Regiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where did the 65th Protection Regiment belong, where did that belong in the structure?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's an independent unit of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Could we have 65 ter 888.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, do you recall basically testifying to that chronology in the Blagojevic case, where you testified about getting to Nova Kasaba, and the prisoners at the 65th, and going to the 65th Protection Regiment base? Do you remember testifying about that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you remember the Defence attorney --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- for Colonel Blagojevic had showed you this particular intercept during that testimony? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so had he shown you this intercept, before you'd actually testified, to help you get ready for the testimony and what you would be testifying about?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So the first time you saw this was when he dropped it on you in the trial?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think it's break time, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. We must have our first break now, and we will resume quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. And, Mr. President, I've cut some material and tried to estimate. And I'm going much slower than I had thought, but I will finish this segment, if that's all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It means a little bit more than one additional hour. Try to do your very best.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Colonel, we had this intercept up on the board, and you recall talking about it in the Blagojevic trial, I'm sure. This is an intercept we received from the Croatian Government. It's a synopsis, as you can see, and it says: "Major Malinic, the commander of the 65th Protective Motorised Regiment, and Colonel Pero Salapura ..." Are you ever called "Pero"?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to my face. Pepo. Maybe some people in Croatia maybe called me Pero some time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you just said "Pepo"?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is Pepo your normal nickname?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be the most oftenly used, but Pero, Pepo, Petar. There are many nicknames in our part of the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, we know that. So now it says "VRS Security Service" in English. Is that what it says in the Serbian, or the Croatian, I should say?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says "Security Service," and it shouldn't be, it should be "Intelligence Service," because Security Service" is "Bezbednost." They've obviously mixed things up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay, so they got that wrong. You said that --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You did say you were at the football field at Kasaba, and this says they were about -- around about 500 prisoners there at the moment. Is that roughly correct? When you were there, were there 500, about?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may, please, I think this was in Konjevic Polje. This football pitch was in Konjevic Polje, not in Kasaba, or am I wrong? But I think it was in Konjevic Polje. It was on the right-hand side. If that's how it was, then, yes, I was not at the football pitch, itself. I just passed by it. And on the way back from Bratunac, I was stopped by a non-commissioned officer, I think, who asked me to go see Malinic again and to pass it on to him that there were certain problems there. Whether it was about water or -- I can't remember now, because I met with Malinic both on my way there and back. But I did not go to the football pitch. I just passed by it, and I was stopped there by this man. And then my conversations with Malinic were at a school, but I think that school is in Kasaba, where the Command of the Military Police Battalion was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you make any effort to communicate with anyone, over telephone or radio, from the base of the 65th Protection Regiment, the Military Police Battalion?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether I talked with someone from that location, no, I don't remember talking to anyone from the base, except directly with Malinic, but I don't remember any other conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what did you learn from Malinic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing. Our first conversation, and I told you about it, was about where General Mladic is, and I was told that General Mladic was in the area of Bratunac. And on my return, I just passed on the information received from his soldiers that they are having problems with water, because it's very hot and they just need more water.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So Malinic told you where Mladic was, and you just went to see Mladic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's correct. From there, I then returned back, and from there, I set off to Bratunac. And I was told there, at the brigade command, that Mladic wasn't there, that he was somewhere in the area of Srebrenica. And I also left the IT people there, and I headed for Srebrenica and Potocari. At first, I thought it was Srebrenica, but later on, in my conversations or during the interview with your investigator, who showed me a photo, I realised I hadn't been in Srebrenica, but in Potocari instead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, before leaving the Kasaba area, where these 500 prisoners were, did you make any effort to see what sort of intelligence information was being gathered from these prisoners or whether there had been any effort -- any organised effort to interview them to get intel?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. First of all, there was no one I would ask. I wouldn't know who to ask. There were only soldiers there. And, secondly, I did not take part in the planning of the operation, not at all. And in the planning, everything gets organised. I cannot get involved, and there would be no purpose in my involvement. There was nothing I could get out from that. It's a system that is functioning, goes from platoon to company, battalion, brigade, and so on and so forth. Everything is well organised. I could not just get out and then go just to the -- I was, you see -- I was chief of administration. It would be silly. I would come to a soldier and say, You, soldier, tell me, and what should I ask them? I didn't even know what to ask. I was not involved in the planning of the operation at all. And as far as Srebrenica, itself, for me and for the Intelligence Administration, Srebrenica was not of any interest. Immediately after the taking of Srebrenica, itself, it became absolutely uninteresting for us. We were interested in the Tuzla Corps and the problems concerning the column that you asked me about. That was something that was under the jurisdiction of military police, MUP, and other organs. Any information, of course, received is passed on, yes, but this was not the focus of our activities, and especially not the focus of my activities. I was there just -- I just happened to be there, and I did not try and get into anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So when you went by the Bratunac Brigade headquarters, did you see any intel person, Momir Nikolic, Radoslav Jankovic, the commander? Did you see any officers there at all?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Well, yes, I ran into -- I don't know who he was, but he was the duty officer of the Bratunac Brigade. And I did ask him about the whereabouts of General Mladic, and he told me that General Mladic was in the area of Srebrenica. I also left the two officers there, and I asked them to -- asked the people there to give them something to eat. I do not remember seeing any of the officers. I did not even know the commander of the brigade there. I didn't know the officers there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Had you learned that Radoslav Jankovic was there from Malinic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not from Malinic. Malinic was commander of the Military Police Battalion. I didn't know where Radoslav Jankovic was at that time. I believed he was up there. Only when I got there, Mamlic told me that Karanovic was on leave, that this one was as I just mentioned, and that he was on his own, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So when you keep saying "up there," so when you got back to Crna Rijeka on that very day, the 13th, that's when you learned Jankovic was in the Bratunac area?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that Jankovic was at the SFOR compound. That's what I was told, I assume upon an order by his commander or maybe General Tolimir, that he was assigned to be the liaison officer of the Drina Corps with the SFOR and that he is at the SFOR compound in -- not in Bratunac, but in - what's it called? - Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when you say "SFOR" --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: As you're aware, SFOR was the name of one of the NATO contingents that was there. The first one in 1996 was IFOR, the next one was SFOR. So when you say "SFOR," what do you mean; UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was first UNPROFOR during the war, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Can we see P01021, starting at 65 ter 888. Oh, excuse me, I didn't offer to tender the last one, 888. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, we have seen on the screen two intercepts, the English interpretation or translation of two intercepts, but you were only dealing with one we have seen in B/C/S. Is it possible to up-load only the -- the translation of that one you, in fact, are tendering?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, it is. It's always been that way, but there's no reason it should be. You're correct, we can just get the one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That one, in both versions, will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit P2205, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And before I play the video: Were you able to see Mladic, shortly after leaving Bratunac, either in Potocari or in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In Potocari, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when you saw him, was there anybody filming? Did you see any film cameras?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, there were more than one people with cameras. There were also journalists there. He was answering questions, giving an interview. They were recording it, and I stood there, about 30 metres away from him, and then he just gave me a sign saying, Wait a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So did you understand that it was likely that you were filmed as well?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I wasn't paying attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's play the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before you do this, perhaps --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Later on, I saw it in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Perhaps I missed something. I recall that you told us you received a secret message in Belgrade, and then you wanted to contact Mladic or Tolimir, is that correct, in order to convey this message?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, that's correct. That's why I was there in the first place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Did you convey this message to General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had that message for him and another or maybe two more proposals. But even as I was conveying him the message and my views on it, we disagreed about certain things. And our conversation was interrupted, and then I got back into my vehicle and headed to Han Pijesak. We had an argument about some items concerning the message, itself, its urgency and the seriousness of the content. General Mladic was elated with the success of the operation. It was completed successfully, without significant casualties and so on. And I told him that that was of lesser importance, that General Krstic should deal with the rest of the situation, and that General Mladic should start dealing with the problems in the west. And then we had kind of a conflict, and then I just turned on my heel and left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sorry for interrupting, Mr. McCloskey. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. We have a film that we believe is from the 13th of July from Serbian Radio and Television, and we'll start it at 40:10. It's P01021.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. We've stopped it at 41:06.1. We see General Mladic has just been chatting with a woman.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you recognise anyone in that photograph besides General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm here, behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, there is -- are you behind the woman in the --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so. Yes, yes, yes, I think that's me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Behind the woman in the white T-shirt?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your face is partially obscured by her head?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was this around the time that you spoke to General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think this was before our conversation, because we started our conversation after everything was recorded. That's at least how I remember things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So did you have --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember this very segment, but it could have been only immediately prior to our conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I think we can just play it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It ended at 00:41:17.5.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, did you have a chance, after that little video-clip we saw, to actually speak to Mladic privately?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke to him personally, if that's what you're asking me. In the clip, there was no conversation between us. But our conversation was not private; it was official.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What I mean, Colonel, is did you talk to him about these important matters, with other people listening, or did you talk to him alone, just you and he?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think his security detail was there. I don't know how many people, how many soldiers, but they were several metres away. This is my best recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when you and your driver went back, did you drive through Potocari on your way?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, roughly, what time of day is it that you're driving back, just very roughly? We see, from the intercept, that they overheard some communication about you being there at about 10.15 at Kasaba, in the morning, so can you give us just a rough gauge on when you would have left to go --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may have been 10.00, Kasaba. It may have been 2.00 p.m. or 1.00 p.m. I cannot be more precise than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when you went through Potocari, did you notice men, old men and young men, being separated from their families?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, there were like elderly men, younger men, women, children, but I did not observe any kind of selection. I did see women and children getting onto the buses, but I wasn't paying too much attention to that. I think they were at the time loading up buses, because there were a few buses there. And, yes, there were many, many, many women and children and elderly people, but I cannot give you any precise numbers either, and there were also our soldiers there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: According to a Bratunac Brigade MP who has testified in this case, he was directed to count the men who were separated from their families by your subordinate, Radoslav Jankovic, who was also in Potocari at that time. Did you see Radoslav Jankovic in Potocari either when you went through the first time or came back on the second time on the 13th?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I haven't seen him at all, and I didn't have any contacts with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you see any bodies --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I also didn't see any of the officers I knew at the time in Potocari. I believe -- at least I haven't noticed any separation going on. I just saw several buses there, and people were entering into the buses. It was before I set off back that I saw people entering the buses, after my conversation with Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When you had your conversation with Mladic, did he tell you about his order to separate the men and have them all killed?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't think he would have said something like that to my face. He certainly wouldn't have said that to my face. If he did issue such an order or anything like that, he would definitely not have said it in front of me. And we -- I just said I had two or three questions to discuss with him, but the conversation was cut off, on the basic question. I had -- about this conversation with the diplomat, I mean, we can go back to that now. When we were talking, he asked me, What's going on in Srebrenica? I told him that I didn't know, that I didn't have any information, that I didn't even know about it. And then we talked about this arrival, that we would see. And he said, You probably have a lot of prisoners, and it would be a good thing to organise that and treat them strictly in the spirit of the Geneva Conventions, and, in a way, we could perhaps help out in changing this image of you that the world has. It was my intention also to talk about that, to convey that to the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Who are you saying is telling you that you have a lot of prisoners and they should be treated according to the Geneva Conventions? Who is saying this to you? You lost me.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I said this is what the diplomat in Belgrade told me. I told you that. Most probably, you will have a lot of prisoners. As for this here, no, this was not discussed at all in the conversation between me and General Mladic, just what we were doing, we did a great job, we completed it all quickly, the operations. He was talking with journalists over there. I think they were waiting for him to give another interview, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you're now saying a Japanese diplomat, on the night of the 12th, told you you probably have a lot of prisoners and you should treat them according to the Geneva Conventions?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and that this should be open and shown to the world, this position of ours, this attitude of ours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. After you go through Potocari, and, as you've said, you didn't see much, I take it you go through Bratunac, and then on to Konjevic Polje, and passed Nova Kasaba, and on to Han Pijesak.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you see anything or talk to anyone of significance?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said I met with Malinic again, I dropped by again on my way back, because when we got there to the intersection where the prisoners were, one of his superiors, a non-commissioned officer, asked me to drop by at -- stop by at the battalion command and to tell them that they were having problems with water, that they didn't have water. So I dropped by there again. I don't know what time it was. It was already the afternoon. I dropped by at Malinic's, at the battalion command, and I conveyed this to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were there more prisoners on the soccer pitch than there were the first time you were there?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prisoners? I don't think so. Well, I didn't really count the first time. I didn't pay attention. There were quite a few, but I couldn't tell you exactly how many. I said that the last time. There was several hundred. I don't know how many. I didn't notice that it was any kind of large number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
