utterances.text: The intercept said "500." Do you disagree with that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really couldn't say. I really wouldn't want to be going back and forth with the number. I couldn't say whether it was 200, 300, 500. I wasn't really paying attention to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What happened to those 500 prisoners?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I am just talking about that -- well, I can say, through the trial proceedings, the reports, that these people were shot, but at that point in time I didn't know what happened. I didn't know what was going on right until the time of the Erdemovic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So what do you learn at the time of the Erdemovic case? And Erdemovic was arrested on March 2nd, 1996, in Belgrade, and his initial appearance at the Tribunal was 31 May 1996.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, already then the media began to write, already when he was arrested in Belgrade, about how members or a group of members from the Sabotage Battalion executed a number of those prisoners and whatnot. And what do I know? And they did mention some numbers. The numbers keep changing from then to now. The numbers range from 3.000 to 8.000, the total number of people who were shot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So are you saying it wasn't until sometime after his arrest on March 2nd, 1996, that you learned that people were murdered by the VRS?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When this was published in the press, then the stories began.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, we have spent quite a bit of time looking at how the 10th Sabotage was used, how it was used in Srebrenica. And what have you learned? How was it used on the 16th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I found out that a group of soldiers was used, not a unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What did you find out?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, I received information that it was three or four soldiers. This was when Erdemovic was arrested. After that, the first headlines in the press appeared. I can't remember the exact date. And then later, everything was published. It was all clear through the proceedings in this Tribunal, and so on and so forth. But then I called Pelemis, the commander of the unit. I was already on vacation or at -- was available, and I asked him whether this was correct, that they participated. And I know that at that time, that a part of the unit was in Modrica and the other part was engaged in combat in Srebrenica, and then they were allowed to have a ten-day rest period. He told me --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Please tell us what Pelemis told you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me that, yes, they did take part, they were engaged. And then I asked him, Did you take part in the ordering? He said he did not, but that the soldiers went voluntarily, that he did not order them to do so. I said that nothing further interested me. The person whose problem it was would then need to resolve the problem subsequently. That's all. I just want -- I told him, I just want to know if you were or weren't. And if you were involved, then you need to face that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So do you really believe that four soldiers went voluntarily and took part in this massive execution? Is that really what you think happened, it was just the four soldiers went voluntarily, no orders given?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, see, I asked Pelemis if he was the one who issued the order, and he told me that he wasn't and that they went voluntarily. And to this day, I don't know exactly what the actual truth is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So, Colonel, what did you learn really happened? Four soldiers don't find their way across the country-side to a mass execution voluntarily.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no, I'm talking about the time -- absolutely. I'm just telling you what I got at that time, what is left. I am not going into the things that I could read about in the press and things that emerged in the trials before this Tribunal up until now. I don't want to go into that. This was something that was already established by the Court. You probably know that so much better than me in a second, in a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Erdemovic has stated that he was able to get an ID to help him get into Serbia. Did you help Erdemovic and others get IDs, well before he got arrested?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What personal ID? I don't know what you're talking about. Whose ID he got?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you help get fake IDs for Erdemovic and other members of the 10th Sabotage Detachment so they could get into Serbia or for other purposes?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Republika Srpska, they had personal ID cards in Republika Srpska, and they, in any event, had them still. I think they were issued to them during the war so that they would be able to move around as citizens. As for fake ones, that is something I don't know, if these were the ones that were issued in Republika Srpska. I don't know about them getting any other kind of IDs. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 7360 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I know that the MUP of Republika Srpska issued them with ID cards.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you wish to change your testimony, sir, before this document comes up on the stand -- up on the screen?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regarding what? Regarding the IDs?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's take a look at this.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is dated 16 January 1996, well before Erdemovic was arrested?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's a document from the Public Security Department head.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And it's to the Main Staff of the VRS, Sector for Intelligence and Security, intelligence information -- for information, and the police say: "Please find enclosed the full text of a dispatch from the Main Staff of the VRS."

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I see it. Yes, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me read it, sir: "... Sector for Intelligence and Security." And they send this thing on. And if we go to the second page, what they send on - could we go to the next page in English - is in your name, so let's see what they say you sent them, because they said they enclosed the full text of the dispatch, as we can see. That was dated 14 January to the Ministry of Interior, to the minister, personally. So you're communicating to him personally: "Considering that we have a group of members of the 10th Sabotage Detachment who are foreign citizens or are on the list of individuals who have been indicted by The Hague Tribunal, we ask that you order the Bijeljina MUP to issue personal IDs with Serbian first names and last names to these individuals, or with different first and last names for Serbian nationals. There are eight such individuals. "They should be reported by the commander of the 10th Sabotage Detachment or the intelligence person from the command of the detachment. "Please inform us about your decision. "Chief, Colonel Petar Salapura." Now --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Drazen Erdemovic, his testimony is that eight members of the 10th Sabotage Detachment took part in this mass execution, and here, sir, you --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I see it here, eight, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I don't need to remind you you're testifying under oath.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But, sir --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am testifying correct, absolutely. Believe me, I do not recall this, but I do accept it, meaning that then I -- yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Colonel, you've --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I am telling you that I was convinced that that's what it was up until this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Colonel, you've testified that you didn't even hear about any of the killings until Erdemovic was arrested, which wasn't until March. You're now, in a document dated January, talking about a list of people in The Hague indictment list, and you're asking for fake --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- IDs for them. So, sir, you are involved in this much more than you're telling us, aren't you? Why don't you tell us the truth? How much are you involved? Just tell us right now. Get it off your chest.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Believe me, I am getting it off my chest. I have nothing to do with that, and I am horrified by it. Today, I'm horrified by it, but I'm not able to connect that to the actual events. It's been quite a while since that time. I think that then, the first information I had about it, then I didn't know that anyone from this unit participated in that. I received information about it down there in Mostar from Safet Orucevic when he told me that there were stories there that people from Srebrenica were killed, a number of them, and so on and so forth, so I cannot really tell you exactly when this was. It was in late 1995, 1996. I really -- couldn't really get a grasp on the number of the people, that something like that was possible, the scale. But here I see that it is the 16th of January, 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right, Colonel, let's go back. You're now --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's when the indictment was issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what time do you get back to Crna Rijeka on the 13th, just roughly again?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And do you see General Mladic that night?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I returned? No, I don't know that I saw him. I don't remember seeing him in Crna Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you receive an intelligence update on what was going on in Srebrenica, and Nova Kasaba, Bratunac, the column going towards Tuzla; anything?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The next morning, on the 14th, I want to ask you about -- we know on the 15th, as you've already told us, that you issued an order to jam the communications of the 28th Division and the 2nd Corps, but let's talk about the 14th. I want to go to --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the jamming, the jamming, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, I want to go to the 14th. The jamming was the 15th, when you're at work, so -- and you've --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would like to tender 65 ter 7360, if I could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Leave is granted to add it to the 65 ter exhibit list, and this document will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit P2206, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Colonel --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I put one question to the witness at this moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, how many letters did you write directly to a minister of your government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How many questions I sent to the minister?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: How many letters did you write directly to a minister of your government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The defence minister, you mean? Which minister?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: A minister, any minister of your government.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I really couldn't say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Did that happen quite often?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember how many I wrote. Not many. I don't remember. Perhaps I sent some to the minister of defence. I don't see any reason to write or of having to write to any other ministers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Was that the normal chain of reporting for you, as a colonel in the army, directly to a minister of your government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it was not customary, unless there was a need for something specific. I don't know. I don't remember what letters I wrote and what the letters were about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And you are still saying that you don't recall this letter about the fake IDs you wrote personally to a minister?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know, and I said that. I know that ID cards were issued to everyone in Republika Srpska, and that I requested that, and that they were issued by the Bijeljina Security Centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, one moment, please. I'm not asking you about the normal procedure to all citizens of Republika Srpska. I'm asking you about this --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- to the minister, personally. This is a quite unusual letter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What was the reason for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, like it said, there are letters. I'm not disputing that. They are there, but I simply don't remember. I know that I did request that ID cards be issued to soldiers who did not have our ID cards. I don't know whether that was then and with this motive here. Please believe me that I don't remember, but that is that. I do accept that. I'm not disputing it, but it's been a lot of time since then, and a person just doesn't remember everything. I wrote a lot of documents and sent them out. I did write frequently to the foreign minister also, also to the Security Services. This was the customary channel of communication. But I don't think that I wrote many letters to the minister of the interior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Did you ever write a letter to the foreign minister, personally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did to a foreign minister, yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Personally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, personally to him, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Were you allowed, as a career officer of the army, to write letters to the foreign minister, personally and directly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, because there was certain information there that was at the same time of interest for me and for him or them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And you didn't send it through your superiors in the chain of command to your commander in the Ministry of Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it didn't go to the Ministry of Defence. It went to them directly from the General Staff, but it was sent once the commander approved it and said that the foreign minister or the president of Republika Srpska would need to be informed about that particular piece of information. Then that kind of information we did send out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Colonel, is there anything about this particular request that you sent to the minister that would have upset your boss, General Tolimir? I mean, we all know what upsets our bosses.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I don't know if Tolimir is informed about this, how can I put it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, just a small correction on page 51, line 16. The exhibit number is, I think, a bit too long.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Colonel, that wasn't my question. You know your boss. You know what you're allowed to do, what you're not allowed to do. Looking at this now, would this have gotten you in trouble with General Tolimir, this request? --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it says "Sector" here. It could be that General Tolimir was not there at the time and that I signed it for that reason. I would not be able to say for sure now, because up at the top it says "Main Staff, VRS, Sector for Intelligence and Security Affairs and Administration of Intelligence, for your information," et cetera. It could be that he wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just for the record, the document number on page 51, line 16, should be P2206. Please carry on, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Colonel, it was a simple question. Would this request, had it been known by General Tolimir, gotten you in trouble with General Tolimir? We all know what gets us in trouble with our bosses, or our Judges, or our spouses.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps it would if it had been sent without his knowledge, but it could also be that he was absent at the time and I sent it out myself. Now, whether he got to know about this subsequently, I really couldn't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Wouldn't General Tolimir have to know about your personal request to a minister to issue fake IDs to people you thought were on the indictment list?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he should have. That's how it should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I really cannot say, one way or another, for sure. That's the way it should be, but I can't be certain now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to an area that I know you've gone over with before in the last trial, so it shouldn't take us too long. And I'd like to go to the exhibit. It should be -- it's the duty officer note-book, and we can give you the original so you can read it clearly in the original. It should be P01459, e-court page 41 in English and page 40 in the B/C/S. And as you'll remember from the last trial, you were shown this duty officer note-book from the Zvornik Brigade, and we should get to the parts that we're talking about. And if you could -- we'll give you the original book, which makes it a lot easier. And you know and we all know --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: 14 July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. What we have on the right side in the English is what we call the teacher's edition, where we have put in some analysis. Now, we know, as do you, that the duty officer of the Zvornik Brigade, like all duty officers, sometimes will take notes on information that comes in. That's his job. And this Major Dragan Jokic was the duty officer on the 14th of July. And it's always difficult to tell in this rough book exactly what time a call came in, but we can see, if we look back in the book, references to some times, but the time doesn't really matter. Dragan Jokic wrote down that: "Colonel Salapura called and that Drago and Beara are to report to Golic." And just to put this in context, on the 14th of July there's significant evidence in this case that Colonel Beara was working with Drago Nikolic, the security officer of the Zvornik Brigade, to transport and murder, by firing squad, thousands of Muslim prisoners held in the Zvornik area. There's also indications that Major Golic was co-ordinating that from Vlasenica by making sure their fuel was issued. And on the 14th, according to the duty officer, you call and pass on the message that Drago and Beara are to report to Golic. So do you recall this? And if so, why on earth, Colonel, are you calling for Beara and Drago Nikolic and having them call Golic in the middle of a genocide?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know what was going on. It's obvious that I was just passing on a message. And it says here not the Beara report to Golic, but to stop at Golic's office. That probably refers to Vlasenica. It depends on the time. It could have been at the time of breakfast or lunchtime, and at that time Mamlic could have gone to Miletic, or called and there was no one, and then I was the one who passed the message, or perhaps a telegram was received at that time and I just passed the telegram on. This could have, perhaps, been a message. I'm not managing to recall it, but I'm just thinking that's the only explanation I can think of. I, myself, have no reason -- would have had no reason to call them directly. It's a completely different service. I could only have passed somebody else's message; for example, that I received a message at the command post, but it could have been a message from Tolimir or from the commander, although the commander's message would probably go through the staff. No, I don't know about this, and I couldn't really explain it otherwise. But it's just a message that was passed on, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's your answer, this is just a message, and you don't know anything about what it was about?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know. You can see from the contents that's how it was in the original, that they should call, and it just didn't contain any more. Now, why they were supposed to call or to go somewhere, for what purpose, I don't know. I just would like to say that the way it's written here doesn't necessarily mean they were to report to Golic, himself, but they were perhaps just wanted in Vlasenica, they were supposed to go see somebody there.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness kindly speak into the microphones, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to page 75 in English and 74 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Colonel, it should be the next tab. We can help you with that, if you'll give it to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this is no longer on the 14th. It's probably on the late night of the 15th, or early morning hours of the 16th. And there's another message: "Drago and Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic are to report to Major Golic early in the morning." Do you have any knowledge about that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- absolutely nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to page 79 in the English and page 78 in the B/C/S, and that should be the next tab for you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's also from this diary?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what I want to direct your attention to is the entry by Milorad Trbic. Do you know who Milorad Trbic was of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. He writes down that at: "0855, Golic asked Popovic to call him, and said that he can forget what he'd asked for and what he wrote about. He knows what he's supposed to do according to the agreed procedure (boss from Panorama 01)." Tell us who Panorama 01 is.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe there is a hotel called Panorama, as far as I remember, near Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you recall the code-name of --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, what "Panorama 01" is, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you recall the code-name of the Main Staff, and "01" being that of the commander, being the relevant code-name at the time?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That code was usually given to the commander, "01."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How about Panorama; do you recall that was the code-name in place in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I know there is a Hotel Panorama.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. We'll refer to the bulk of the other evidence on that. And it says: "Message conveyed to Popovic at 9.10." And then at the bottom of the page, we see: "Beara to call Panorama at 155." Do you remember whose extension 155 was at the Crna Rijeka Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't remember anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Would it help you if I said that was Milovanovic's extension that was being used by Miletic at the time and rang in the operations room?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, operations room, could be.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to English, 85; B/C/S, 84. It should be the next tab in the book and the last entry I'll ask you about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we see here, on the 16th of July, that someone called in, and the duty officer, again Trbic, noted down that: "At 1400 hours, Popovic requested a bus with a full tank and 500 litres of D2." D2 is diesel fuel; correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, diesel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And: "... the Zlatar duty officer and Golic informed." Do you remember which unit Zlatar was the code-name for?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. That's an internal code-name within the Drina Corps for some brigades or units, but I don't know these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Would you recall that that is -- Zlatar was the code-name for the Drina Corps at the time?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never used it in my communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You were on duty on the 16th of July, and, sir, there's significant evidence in this case that at this time Popovic was organising the transportation from the Branjevo -- or from this school at Pilica to the Branjevo Farm, where Erdemovic and the 10th Sabotage Unit were summarily executing over a thousand men, and there's documents showing that Popovic received that fuel, going to Pilica. There's evidence in this case, and it shows Golic involved, it shows Popovic involved, it shows Beara involved. And so if we go back to your notation at 14 July, where you are telling Beara and Drago to report to Golic, this suggests you are involved, sir. Having looked at all this material, tell us --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I just received a message about which I knew nothing. I don't know who it came from. It could have come from -- I don't remember now from whom it was received. It must have been during lunchtime, when there was no one around, when I was in the dining hall alone. And during meal times, Warrant Officer Nedeljkovic and both of my IT men, they all went out for lunch, and I was the only one who stayed there. And it was the only time that message could have come, and I forwarded it. I did not pass on other messages. That would normally have been done by Mamlic or someone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You were in Nova Kasaba on the 13th. You were with Mladic on the 13th. You were at Crna Rijeka on the 13th, the 14th, the 15th, the 16th and the 17th; correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. On the 14th, I also went to see a doctor, and on the 17th as well, and came back.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What was General Tolimir's nickname?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nickname? Apart from "Zdravko" and "Tolimir," I believe the commander called him "Tolja." I don't know of any other nicknames.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We heard over and over here that some people were able to call him "Toso."

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, right. "Toso" is short for "Tolimir," but that nickname would have been used by the commander and the superior officers --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And Miletic, was he sometimes called "Mico"?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Milovanovic called him "Mico," as far as I heard. I never called him "Mico."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to P394. 394B, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This should not be broadcast because it's under seal, I'm informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, this will come up on the screen, but I can set the scene. This is one of these intercepts from the Bosnian Army. This is dated 16 July at 10 hours. This was the day that the 10th Sabotage Detachment was murdering people at the Branjevo Farm, and the participants are noted as Mico and Toso. And Toso says: "I sent you, you know what, over there via Uran, and you send it to me via Uran, because this one is not secure." Do you remember what "Uran" stood for back then?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. It's the first I hear of it, Uran. It must be that certain code-names were assigned during the operation, and I'm telling you, I never participated either in the planning or any of the tasks, nor did I have any of these code-names or call-names or call-signs. I didn't know what they meant. It's a code-name for something. Now, for what, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I believe we have a little problem with the electronic courtroom, because the versions in English and the Serbian are not consistent. It's a completely different intercept, as far as I can see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, check that, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, here --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. As we remember the nature of these reports, we have to go --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I see "Mico" and "Toso."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, now I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, if this is between Miletic and Tolimir, and we have a document which I may be able to show later, if not, that is -- like you say, is the attack plan for Srebrenica, and it says "Uran" is the code-name for the Drina Corps forward command post, which on the 16th was at a place called Krivace, do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Near Krivace? No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You don't remember the Drina Corps forward command post for the Zepa attack?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I've never been there and I don't know where their command post was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Maybe you can help us. When Tolimir says: "Send it to me via Uran, via the Drina Corps Command IKM, because this one is not secure," what's he referring to? What isn't secure?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe he meant that the line was not secure, that it's an open communication, probably a radio-relay one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And then Miletic says, if "Mico" is Miletic: "All right." And then Tolimir says: "And tell Pepo."

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know who that would have been?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then M says: "Yes. Toso says: "If, that I received what he sent me, and if he wants to send me something, he can call Uran on the same line that you are communicating with Uran, and he can relay the telegram for me through it, and you know my call sign." And M says: "Uh-huh, okay. Did Uran asked you over this, I mean that line regarding some information check?" And then Toso says: "About?" And they go on a bit. I won't read all of it. And then Tolimir says: "He was supposed to send them this morning. He received it 20 minutes ago." M says: "I'm going to call him and check why he didn't send it yet." Tolimir says: "Call him, and tell Pepo and my" something, "that they can send me telegrams this way and I can send it to them." And then they say: "Good." "Goodbye." And then the operator hears: "Five minutes later, Mico called Jevdo on this frequency ... and asked about two telegrams he was supposed to forward him." They agreed that Jevdo was going to send them immediately. So this is involving you sending secure information to Tolimir, isn't it, on the 16th of July?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, a moment ago this record -- this document was not read correctly. It says "Pepo and my" or "their people," because if I say, Tell Pepo and these men of his, it should be read correctly for the record. I would like to see the page back again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, we should have the page back. We see in the English translation that there was a doubt. If the interpreters could read and interpret it in the correct way, and, therefore, I think Mr. McCloskey left this word out. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says "those men of mine." Why don't you tell them, Aleksandar? You know English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think the general is correct. The interpreter thought it might have said "men." But they know their own expressions better than our interpreters do, so I'll take their word for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, "Jevdo" on this second page, did you know the Drina Corps coms fellow Jevdjevic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment. Let me see. Oh, Jevdjo, Jevdjo. I don't know who that is. Maybe Jevdjevic. I don't know who he was referring to. Was there anyone else with a similar nickname? This is most probably an abbreviated surname, maybe also first name. It may have been Jevdjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who was Jevdjevic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Communications man.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: For who?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a communications officer. He was part of the Communications Regiment of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So you've had a chance to look at this, and you've told us what it's about.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us any more about what -- what kind of information were you passing on to General Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not be able to tell you, with any degree of certainty, what it was about. It must have been something about the reasons why I came to see General Mladic. It could have been only that that I could convey. And I remember having been told that any communications with him should go via the Rogatica Brigade, and this shows that it must have been done via some other location, maybe the forward command post, but I cannot say this with any degree of certainty. A telegram was sent, because he didn't even know that I was there before that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So do you stand by that this is an authentic intercept?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot say for certain, yes, this is authentic, but it seems logical. This kind of conversation seems logical, but I cannot claim that. I wasn't the one intercepting the conversation, you see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's logical for the chief of intel and security to be communicating with his chief of intel and telling him how to best get confidential information to him? Nothing unusual about that, I take it.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there would be no reason for that. If this would be -- go along a certain line, and if he knew what the nods were -- I guess if he knew that this was an open line, he was just warning that documents should not be sent that way, but via the forward command post instead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I have one more document that's on this same subject, and then I'll be through, Mr. President. So I don't know if people can go another couple of minutes, or I can do it after --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We're already beyond the six hours. How many minutes do you need with this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It should just be a couple, just a few. It's just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Shall we finish with that before the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would like to, if we could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It could speed up the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Could we have 65 ter -- 65 ter 4052, D49. Thank you to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, sir, this is -- all we have is a handwritten document, and it's -- as we can see, it's from the Command of the Drina Corps, the forward command post at Krivace. This is the next day from the intercept. It's 17 July, and it's entitled "A radio conversation with Avdo Palic," and it's under the name of Zdravko Tolimir. Do you recognise the handwriting at all? --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, this handwriting --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So we see here that -- does it appear to you that General Tolimir is communicating from the forward command post at Krivace, or at least he's sending his communications out from that area?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The command -- yes, it says here "the Command of the Drina Corps, Forward Command Post Krivace."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So do you agree that this appears that he would be sending his communications out from that -- on this day, anyway, he would send out this information from Krivace?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. I have nothing further, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, yes, this was sent, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We must have the second break now. Mr. Gajic, before we break, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, here in the transcript, on page 68, line 3, "65 ter 4052, D49," D49 is a completely different document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is confirmed by the Registrar. But in the list of documents we received from the Prosecution, the last update, it is said that this should be the same one. I propose this should be checked during the break. Thank you very much. We adjourn, and resume at 20 minutes past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, before we adjourned, we had a discussion about a number of a certain document. I was told that a mistake occurred in that respect. Could you clarify that for the record?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. It should have been 65 ter 4052, and it's not D -- ignore the "D." It should be 65 ter 4052, so I guess it needs a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And did you tender it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Apparently, I didn't, and I should.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In that case, it will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit P2207, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now it's the turn of Mr. Tolimir to put questions to you, sir, during his cross-examination. Mr. Tolimir, I have noted that your estimate for cross-examination of this witness is eight hours. The Prosecution has used a little bit more than six hours. You will recall that our fellow Judge, Judge Mindua, referred you to the practice of other Chambers with respect to the use of time to be used for cross-examination. That was on the 14th of April. It's on page 12789 of the transcript. As you will recall, Judge Mindua gave a short overview of the way other Chambers deal with this issue in this respect. In most cases, the time for examination-in-chief and for cross-examination of viva voce witnesses has been kept in balance. Therefore, I would like to remind you, Mr. Tolimir, that while we will not limit your cross-examination from the outset, as this is a very relevant witness, we will, however, pay close attention to whether you use your time with this witness efficiently by focusing on only relevant issues related to the charges against you. Please keep that in mind. Now you may commence your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Once again, I want to greet everyone in the courtroom, including Mr. Salapura. I would like to thank him for coming here. I'm pleased to see him, and I would like to ask him for a favour. After I have said something, he should check the screen, and when he sees that everything is entered, then, and only then, start answering, because otherwise we'd be overlapping and it will not be reflected in the transcript. And it's very important to have everything recorded in the transcript. So at the end of my question, I will say, Thank you. Then you wait for a few seconds, and then provide your answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, please, Mr. Salapura, the Prosecutor was asking you about Uran. On page 67, line 10, the Prosecutor asked you whether it was logical for Tolimir to be asking his subordinates not to send telegrams via open line, and you said, Yes. Now, tell me, was there anything in the telegrams that can be described as criminal or do they have, as their contents, only elements that refer to combat activities?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The telegrams that we were receiving? Are you referring to those telegrams that we were receiving during the period when I was there at the command post?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I was referring to telegrams that I was sending to you or the ones you were sending to me via this station, Uran, that's at the Command of the Drina Corps and which I would get in touch with, and you can tell us whether the forward command post of the Drina Corps, whether they could have a protected communication channel with Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think there were many such telegrams; maybe one or two only that were received at the command post and that you had sent. As far as I remember, they were sent very seldom. From me, I think only one telegram was sent to you, and it involved a summary of the information I had presented to the commander so that you would also be made aware about the Croatian offensive against the VRS. And it is normal -- it's obligatory to use protected communication. That was a rule whenever there was combat activity going on, if possible. If it was not possible, we would be normally using a TKT code book for the purpose of protecting information for the short period of the duration of combat activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Salapura. Since you were absent, on sick leave, during that period, tell me, do you know whether there was a phone line that had a code-name, Uran, and which could be used by the corps commander to send open messages, verbal messages, and then communication would send those to the addressee, and in such a way the communications would be protected?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember this code-name Uran.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have any memory concerning a phone that can receive a verbal message, and then that the operator who's there could type this as a -- into a written message and then forward it to the addressee? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was possible. You know well that we had two phones which also had operators/encoders, and they would scramble the direct open type of information and send it encoded. We had those as part of our service.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Our sector, our administration, could we request for such protection in relation to conversations which, as its topic, had date on units and activities?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of our information was encoded, was protected.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In this telegram, it is stated: "Mico, tell Pepo and my people." In a conversation, when you say "Pepo," does that also involve the institution that Pepo is at the head of?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say this to the Prosecutor, but that was the practice that you were using. I wasn't sure about that, but thank you for opening this topic. For instance, in the telegram, when it is stated that somebody should go and talk to Pajo or report to Pajo, that does not necessarily mean to Pajo, himself, but to his location in Vlasenica. Or when you say, "Cedo," that may mean just something that helps you with the location because that person is at that location. So this wasn't necessarily something that referred to myself, personally, but to the administration. That was the practice that you were using. That wasn't my practice. I had different practices in that respect, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It may be a translation issue, but they're both now referring to what was an intercept as a telegram, and there's no reference to the 65 ter number. So if we don't correct that, it's going to lead to a problem in the record, because I know they're talking about the intercept that we just talked about with Pepo and Mico.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, could you clarify that with the witness? Are you referring to an intercept?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Salapura, you were shown a text of an intercept. I don't know anything about it, of course. And in that intercept, there is a quotation of my words to Mico. Apparently, I said, Tell Pepo to ... and so on. Does that "Pepo" necessarily refer to the person or it can also refer to the location?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was obviously something that involved an open telephone or radio communication channel, and you were referring to the administration. And I'm saying this on the basis of your custom of the way -- how you expressed yourself throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Salapura. I would like to have P2206 on the screen. It's the document that's dated 16th of January, 1996.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: While this is coming up, I would like to make a correction for the record. It was recorded wrongly in page 51, line 9. It should read "65 ter 7360," instead of "7360" [sic].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Tolimir, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Salapura, the Prosecutor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. It's wrongly recorded again. I said: "'65 ter 7360' instead of '3760.'" Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Salapura, you can see the document that was shown to you also by the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You know the content, so this is my question: In this document, were you trying to cover up or hide anything from the law enforcement organs or were you trying to make sure that people know that they were under surveillance, maybe?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. The problem -- based on the date, 16th of January, I can now say here in this courtroom that since maybe 2001, certain problems with remembering numbers and dates, I was thinking about the 16th, and in my head it's turned into March. I had a mild stroke, and I am having problems because of that. And whenever people are asking me about dates and times, in other words, information, including numbers, I'm having problems. But, yes, this telegram was sent openly to the Ministry of the Interior, but I believed -- I thought it was not sent there. I insisted that it should be sent directly to Bijeljina. However, it seems that they sent it to the Ministry of the Interior. They sent an official request. This was not sent for the purpose of hiding anything. It had a completely different purpose. These soldiers, one of them was a Muslim, the others were Croats, some of them. There were some Serbs as well, but I don't know how many. The total number is eight, as we can see here. I really believed this was something that happened at a later date, but now I can see the date, and I really thought about it for a long time. This was sent because the persons in question had residence in Bijeljina. People from Bijeljina didn't know them because they were not from Bijeljina. And while all this was going on, the idea was to make sure that they do not get exposed to problems that maybe their neighbours would cause or something like that. It was easy to find them later on. Journalists found them very soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell us if you were entrusted by the commander of the Main Staff to secure personal ID cards for persons who were in the units, the reconnaissance and sabotage units, with other names when they are going to alien territory, to provide them with names, and that you had addressed the Ministry of Interior several times on this topic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did have a task to issue us with ID documents, but I think that this is not such a case. I think that this was issued for a different purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. This is why I asked you. Was any crime concealed here? Did you provide their actual names when you sought out the names for them?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, their actual names and particulars were provided. Secondly, when they were going to execute a task, then they would receive a completely different type of identification documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was this immediately after the signing of the Dayton Accords, before even the 120 days had passed, which was the dead-line for the separation of the forces after the signing of the agreement? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know exactly when the 120 days were expiring. The Dayton Accords were signed in November; is that right? Right. Well, I don't know whether that was 120 days or not. Evidently, it wasn't. It wasn't yet six months.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Salapura. You were asked here a number of times if you had sent personal letters to the minister of foreign affairs, in the same way that you have here addressed the minister of the interior. Can you please answer this question: Were you authorised by the commander and by the president of the republic to provide information of interest for the negotiations on the Contact Group to the foreign minister, who was the chief of that delegation that was in charge of contacts with international representatives who were mediating in the drafting of a peace agreement?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't explain that. I felt that there was no need to explain that, because I don't see anything controversial there. I did have that authority, because my sector was dealing not only with the gathering of military intelligence, but also of political intelligence, diplomatic and other types of intelligence or data, so that spectre was also there -- that spectrum was also there. So there were tasks which were not of interest either to the commander of the Main Staff or to the chief of the sector, but which were exclusively of interest to the ministers of foreign affairs, or the interior, or some other ministry. We acquired information that could be of interest to the Ministry of Trade, or some other ministries, or for the president of Republika Srpska. So I was able to provide such information directly, and I did. And this was received by the chief of the sector, Mr. Tolimir, and it was also received by the commander if it was of interest to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Salapura. You were asked here about whether you interrogated prisoners of war that you saw on the playground? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never interrogated a single prisoner of war throughout the entire war. I myself, personally, I never did that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would now like to have 00672 shown to the witness now. This is intelligence support to the armed forces. This is a rule from 1987.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And while we're waiting for this rule to appear on the screen, can you please tell us this: In the Army of Republika Srpska, did we use the rules from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because we didn't have rules of our own. It wasn't only us who used it. The others used it too; the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina; the Croatian Army, too, until they drafted their own rules.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now show page 67 of the document now, please, so that we can see the section that pertains to prisoners of wars. This is Article 198, page 67.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is no 198. There is 158.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 198, the interrogation of prisoners of war. Can the e-court please show --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But that's not on page 67.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, I apologise. It's on page 74. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Which page in English, Mr. Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's page 59 in the English. Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you. And we are now looking at the paragraph 198, which states: "Intelligence organs in commands and staff question prisoners of war and defectors for the purpose of gathering intelligence, through organs of certain specialty that are set up especially for that purpose."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is: If the Drina Corps were to capture or have prisoners and defectors, would the Main Staff then have to interrogate them, or somebody from the Main Staff, or would this be done by the organ that had captured them and in whose corps they happened to be, or would this be done by the intelligence organ of the relevant corps? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This would, of course, be done by the intelligence organ of the corps, starting from the level of battalion up, depending on the importance of the person and the data that that person would be able to offer. Perhaps the security organ would also participate if they felt that it was an interrogation of interest, or some other organ, perhaps if it was a question of the police or some kind of special service or logistics, if it was believed that the person had intelligence data that was relevant for those services. Only exceptionally would somebody participate from the Main Staff. I actually never interrogated anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And since we are looking at this rule, the intelligence support for the armed forces, and in view of the fact that you were the most qualified and the most highly-trained person to be able to interpret these documents and rules, I would kindly ask you to tell the Trial Chamber what is intelligence support of the armed forces. What does that term mean? And until then, can we look at page 12, please. This is page 9 in the English. Thank you, Aleksandar. We're now looking at paragraph 2 or Article 2 of the general provisions, and it states: "Intelligence support in the armed forces is a part of the overall measures, procedures and activities aimed at preparing the society for all people's defence and social self-protection ..." And so on and so forth. My question is: All our actions and activities, were they all a part of those overall general measures undertaken by a society, such as Republika Srpska, and the Army of Republika Srpska, or its armed organisation, in order to provide support for the armed forces? Are they just measures and actions and activities?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've already described what intelligence support means when the Prosecutor, Mr. McCloskey, asked me to describe my work, and I actually did refer to the elements precisely from this Article 2. Yes, of course. And what you're asking also is right. It means the collection of all kinds of information about the enemy, combat actions, the terrain, everything in the area on the other side of the front-line, and, of course, the overall measures and information that is of general interest for the society, for the state, or Republika Srpska specifically, that we had from all the other spheres that could possibly provide certain input and would be conducive to completing the war and implementing the goals and achieving successes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Salapura. Can you please tell us whether intelligence support is part of the command staff function, primarily?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Let us now look at -- I deliberately did not want to go into this, but let us look at Article 4 which states that -- can we please scroll this up so you can see Article 4. This is the following page in the English and the last page in the Serbian. It states: "Intelligence support is part of the command and staff function. The content of intelligence support is a constant process, whose intensity varies and which includes the following ..." And now they list, on the following pages, what all of that implies.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is this: Did the staffs and commands exclusively operate pursuant to the rules as they are described in this article of the rules for the intelligence support of the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in some places, these rules were adhered to. In some places, not, because in some organs, for example, the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, we didn't have the full strength, so these duties were unassigned. For example, sometimes we would assign a certain section or person to be carrying out this intelligence function.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, you were asked by the Prosecutor, in the summary, when you saw Tolimir, and you said, We were together at a seminar in Knin. Can you please tell the Trial Chamber now if we belong to the same military organisation at that time and the same military district, you and I?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up until then, we did not. But after that time -- actually, immediately prior to that seminar, yes, we did. Before that, we did not. You were in part of the military naval district VPO, and this was in Croatia. You were part of the VPO, and then towards the end -- at the end, yes, yes, and when the negotiations were over, then this division became part of the 5th Military District at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean that then, when we saw each other, both of us were in different military districts -- we were both in the 2nd Military District?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct, we were both in the 2nd military district.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In his summary, the Prosecutor asked you whether you had in Vukovar, and you said, No, I was in Zagreb, and I was performing such and such duties. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you now, please, please, tell the Trial Chamber where Vukovar and Zagreb were separate military districts, and could you have had any powers at all in Vukovar, and the other way around, could anyone from Vukovar have any powers in relation to units of the 5th Corps which were in Zagreb? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. Vukovar was in the 1st Military District, the Belgrade Military District, and the 5th Military District could not have any powers there. The border was just like the state border, and it applied in context -- in the context of any military activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you able to tell us when and why you had to be transferred, with your command, to Sarajevo from the Zagreb 5th Military District? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, the command was blocked, the one in Zagreb, and for a long time it was completely isolated, with all of its communications cut off. And every evening, there was firing at that facility, at the building, by the Croatian forces and the MUP and the ZNG, so we were constantly exposed to fire. Then an agreement was reached about pulling the men out of Zagreb, and this was carried out from Slunj. This was already the end of the war in Croatia, when an agreement was already reached on a truce, and then the command was transferred from there to Kosara. And this is where it was renamed as the 2nd Military District.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you able to tell us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, we are at the end of today's hearing. We should continue tomorrow. But tell me, are you going to use this document we have on the screen during your further cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you. I was just about to ask what the area of responsibility is, as described in Article 5, that was under the jurisdiction of Mr. Salapura, to tell us about that zone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is that the intelligence jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, briefly, if I may be allowed, I can answer that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I have already indicated we have to adjourn for the day. I just want to know if you're tendering this document now or if you are going to use it tomorrow any further. Okay, I see you are nodding. We don't have to discuss anything else. We adjourn for the day. I have to remind you, sir, that you are not permitted to have conversation about the content of your testimony with either party during the break. We adjourn, and resume tomorrow, in the afternoon, in Courtroom II, I think, at 2.15. We adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
